job.style: a rule explained with two contrasting examples

response.passage: In geometry, understanding the properties of lines and angles requires precision. A line is defined as having no endpoints, extending infinitely in both directions, whereas a line segment is a distinct part of a line with two fixed endpoints. When two lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles formed are always equal, not supplementary. For example, if two lines cross and one angle is 70 degrees, the angle opposite to it is also 70 degrees, not 110 degrees. Furthermore, the sum of the interior angles of any triangle is always exactly 180 degrees, regardless of the triangle's size or whether it is acute, right, or obtuse. Consider a tiny triangle and a massive triangle drawn on a large field; both will have an angle sum of 180 degrees. Finally, for two lines to be considered parallel, they must never meet, even if extended infinitely. This property holds true regardless of their orientation; lines can be parallel whether they are horizontal, vertical, or tilted at an angle. If a transversal cuts two lines, they are only parallel if specific conditions, such as equal corresponding angles, are met. Visual appearance is never enough to confirm parallelism; geometric proof is required.
response.summary: Lines extend infinitely while segments have endpoints, and vertically opposite angles are always equal. All triangles have an angle sum of 180 degrees regardless of their size. Parallel lines never meet, and their status must be proven rather than assumed by sight.
